rationale: B wins because it finds the fourth usable protagonist: the retailer format. "Sephora at Kohl's gets Glossier: what the shop-in-shop deal says about where the brand wants to sell" is not just another envelope around the door count; it names a trade reporter's actual obsession and demands the door split that would make it real. A is clean and usable, but "A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" sells the fragrance/distribution connection before it has proof, then admits the two facts may just be sharing a date.
gaps_in_A: "collapse of the direct-to-consumer thesis" is too big for one company's unnumbered "fastest-growing channel" claim; the set flags the missing number, but the framing is still overfed.
"covering the wave of beauty brands extending into scent" imports a trend the update does not supply. Without category evidence, that is decoration wearing a press badge.

"A brand born from a beauty blog is now betting on the perfume aisle" makes the product/retail link sound proven before the proof list admits it needs evidence that fragrance belongs on the expanded shelf.
It leaves "Sephora at Kohl's" folded into the scale angle instead of testing whether that format is a separate retail story.
gaps_in_B: "Story type: customer-story" on the Sephora at Kohl's angle is mislabeled. There is no customer outcome here; it is a retailer-format or merchandising angle.
"in one step" implies rollout timing the fact block does not give. B asks for the timeline later, but the argument should not borrow certainty from reporting it has not done.
"where the brand wants to sell" infers intent from door inclusion. Plausible, but still an inference that needs a Glossier or merchant voice before pitching hard.
The Kohl's angle is useful but fragile: "It only stands apart if the Kohl's door count is real and material" is the right caveat, and it means the angle may collapse after one fact check.
